summary: This memo gives criteria for designing a border router that runs BGP with routers outside its network and OSPF inside it, so routes pass correctly between the two. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC is about the router at the edge of a network, where two routing protocols meet. It says which routes may cross the boundary in each direction, what the inside protocol's tag field has to contain so that the outside protocol can rebuild the path information, and how the next hop address is chosen.

questions: how do bgp and ospf interact
how do bgp and ospf exchange routes
what is the ospf external route tag
should bgp routes be imported into ospf
subtitle: The rules a border router follows when it passes routes between the protocol outside and the protocol inside.

tldr.problem: A router that speaks BGP to its neighbours and OSPF inside its own network has to decide which routes to pass in each direction, what values to give them, and what to tell the outside world about where they go.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets defaults for both directions, none exported and none imported unless the administrator says so, and defines how the 32-bit OSPF external route tag carries the information needed to rebuild the BGP ORIGIN and AS_PATH attributes when a route is passed back out.
tldr.outcome: The document was a republication of RFC 1364 with editorial corrections, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic. No later RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: What This Document Decides
sections.content:
The document defines the criteria to be used when designing an Autonomous System Border Router that will run BGP with other border routers external to the autonomous system, and OSPF as its interior gateway protocol. It defines how three pairs of fields and attributes are to be set when the two protocols meet at a border router: the OSPF cost and type against the BGP INTER-AS METRIC, the OSPF tag against the BGP ORIGIN and AS_PATH attributes, and the OSPF Forwarding Address against the BGP NEXT_HOP attribute.

The document uses two terms. An Autonomous System is the term used in the BGP specification, where the use of the term stresses that, even when multiple interior protocols and metrics are used, the administration of an autonomous system appears to other autonomous systems to have a single coherent interior routing plan and presents a consistent picture of what networks are reachable through it. From the standpoint of exterior routing, an autonomous system can be viewed as monolithic, so reachability to networks directly connected to it must be equivalent from all its border routers. A Routing Domain is a collection of routers which coordinate their routing knowledge using a single instance of a routing protocol.

The memo is a republication of RFC 1364 with some editorial problems corrected, and it follows the conventions of the Host Requirements RFCs when using the words MUST, SHOULD and MAY.
sections.plainLanguage: At the edge of a network, an outside protocol and an inside protocol have to agree on what a route means. This RFC sets out the three places where they have to line up: the cost, the path information, and the next hop.

sections.title: Exporting and Importing Routes
sections.content:
BGP does not carry subnet information in routing updates, so when a subnetted network in the OSPF routing domain is referred to in BGP, the equivalent network route is used, and multiple subnet routes are collapsed into one network route when exported into BGP.

For exporting OSPF routes into BGP, the administrator must be able to export routes selectively through a filter mechanism that supports control down to a single network, and must be able to filter on the OSPF tag and its sub-fields. The default must be to export no routes from OSPF into BGP, while a single configuration parameter must permit all OSPF inter-area and intra-area routes to be exported. OSPF external routes of type 1 and type 2 must never be exported into BGP unless they are explicitly configured. When configured to export a network, the border router must advertise a network route for a subnetted network as long as at least one subnet in it is reachable via OSPF.

The network administrator must be able to configure the BGP INTER-AS METRIC statically for any network route, and by default it must not be set, because it is an optional attribute in BGP. The reason is that the two metrics are of different widths: the OSPF cost is a two level metric while the BGP INTER-AS METRIC is only an optional non-transitive attribute, so a more complex mapping between them is not necessary. When a route advertised to external BGP neighbours becomes unreachable, the information must be propagated to those neighbours immediately. An implementation must also have a mechanism setting a minimum time between learning a route via OSPF and advertising it via BGP; the default value is 0, meaning the route is advertised instantly.

For importing BGP routes into OSPF, implementations should allow an autonomous system to control the announcements of BGP-learned routes, with control down to a single network and also to an autonomous system, either the one that originated the route or the adjacent one that advertised it. The default must be to export no routes from BGP into OSPF, so administrators must configure every route they wish to import, though a configuration parameter may allow all BGP routes to be imported. The administrator must be able to configure the OSPF cost and metric type of every imported route; the cost must default to 1 and the metric type to type 2.

Routes learned via BGP from peers within the same autonomous system must not be imported into OSPF, and the border router must never generate a default route into the OSPF routing domain unless explicitly configured to do so. The recommended method for originating default routes is to let the administrator specify a set of network route, AS_PATH, default route cost and default route type tuples: if the router learns of the network route for an element of the set with the corresponding AS_PATH, it generates a default route into the OSPF routing domain with that cost and type, and the lowest cost default route is the one injected.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing crosses the boundary unless the administrator asks for it. When something does cross, the inside cost and type can be set by hand, and the outside metric is usually left unset because it means something different on each side.

sections.title: The BGP Identifier and the OSPF Router ID
sections.content:
The BGP identifier must be the same as the OSPF router ID at all times that the router is up, and the document gives two reasons for this.

The first is synchronisation between OSPF and BGP. Consider three border routers, RT1, RT2 and RT3, in the same autonomous system running OSPF. Both RT1 and RT2 have routes to an external network X and import it into the OSPF routing domain, while RT3 advertises the route to network X to other external BGP speakers. RT3 must use the OSPF router ID to determine whether it is using RT1 or RT2 to forward packets to network X, and hence build the correct AS_PATH to advertise to external speakers. More precisely, RT3 must determine which border router it is using to reach network X by matching the OSPF router ID for its route to network X with the BGP identifier of one of the border routers, and use the corresponding route for further advertisement to external peers.

The second reason is convenience: it is convenient for the network administrator looking at a border router to correlate different BGP and OSPF routes based on the identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Give the router one number and use it for both protocols. Then a router that has to advertise a route to the outside can work out which of its internal neighbours will actually carry the traffic.

sections.title: The OSPF Tag and the BGP Path Attributes
sections.content:
The OSPF external route tag is a 32-bit field attached to each external route, which may be used to communicate information between autonomous system boundary routers. OSPF imports information from various routing protocols at all its border routers, and in some instances it is possible to use protocols other than EGP or BGP across autonomous systems. It is important in BGP to differentiate between routes that are external to the OSPF routing domain but must be considered internal to the autonomous system, and routes that are external to the autonomous system. Routes that are internal to the autonomous system and that may or may not be external to the OSPF routing domain will not come to the various BGP speakers from other BGP speakers within the same autonomous system via BGP, so border routers running BGP must have knowledge of this class of routes in order to advertise them to external autonomous systems without waiting for BGP updates from other speakers inside the same autonomous system.

The document uses the external route tag field in OSPF to set the ORIGIN and AS_PATH attributes in BGP intelligently. Both are well-known, mandatory attributes in BGP. When the Automatic bit of the tag is set to 1, the tag holds a Completeness bit, a two-bit PathLength field, 12 bits of ArbitraryTag that default to 0, and 16 bits holding the autonomous system number of the route, which is 0 if the route is to be considered part of the local autonomous system. When the Automatic bit is 0, the remaining 31 bits are LocalInfo, an arbitrary value configured by the network administrator.

The Completeness bit is set when the source of the incoming route is known precisely, for instance from an interior protocol inside the local autonomous system or from EGP at one of the boundaries, and it refers to the status of the path information carried by the routing protocol. The PathLength field says whether the AS_PATH the protocol could have carried was of length zero, one, or greater than one: routes imported from an interior protocol usually have an AS_PATH of length 0, routes imported from EGP have one of length 1, and protocols that support complete path information indicate a path greater than one.

The OSPF tag is not wide enough to carry path information about routes with a path length greater than one, so that information has to be carried by BGP to the other border routers inside the same autonomous system, and such routes must not be exported from OSPF into BGP. The Automatic bit must default to 0 for backward compatibility, and nothing may be inferred about the characteristics of an OSPF route from the tag bits unless the tag was automatically generated. The value PathLength 11 is reserved, and routers must not generate such a tag; border routers must ignore tags that indicate it.
sections.plainLanguage: When a route comes in from outside, the inside protocol has nowhere to put the path information, so the tag field carries a summary of it instead. Three small bits in the tag say whether the path is known exactly, and how long it was, which is enough to rebuild the origin and the path when the route goes back out.

sections.title: Forwarding Address and the NEXT_HOP Attribute
sections.content:
Forwarding addresses are used to avoid extra hops between multiple routers that share a common network and that speak different routing protocols with each other. Both BGP and OSPF have equivalents of forwarding addresses: in BGP it is the NEXT_HOP attribute, a well-known and mandatory attribute, and in OSPF it is a Forwarding address field.

The document works through a four-router situation. RT1 and RT2 are in one autonomous system, RT3 and RT4 are in another, RT1 and RT3 speak BGP with each other, and RT3 and RT4 speak OSPF with each other, with RT1 and RT2 on a common network with the other two.

For importing a network X that was learnt via BGP from RT1, RT3 must always fill the OSPF Forwarding Address with the BGP NEXT_HOP attribute for the route to network X. For exporting a network Y that is internal to the OSPF routing domain, where RT3's route to network Y is via RT4 and network Y is to be exported via BGP to RT1, if network Y is not a subnetted network RT3 must fill the NEXT_HOP attribute for network Y with the address of RT4. That is to avoid requiring packets to take an extra hop through RT3 when traversing the autonomous system boundary, and it is similar to the concept of indirect neighbour support in EGP.
sections.plainLanguage: When a route is passed on, the next hop is written as the router that will really forward the packets, not as the router that learned the route. That saves a pointless detour across the boundary.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says in one line that security issues are not discussed in it. What it does contain are the administrative safeguards that surround the exchange: routes are only exported or imported when the administrator configures them, the default in both directions is to exchange nothing, and routes whose path information is too long for the tag field must not be exported from OSPF into BGP at all, because the information would be lost.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says nothing about security. Its own protections are administrative: nothing crosses the boundary by accident.

fields.name: Automatic
fields.desc: Set to 1 when the router generated the other sub-fields itself.

fields.name: Completeness
fields.desc: Set when the source of the incoming route is known precisely.

fields.name: PathLength
fields.desc: Whether the AS_PATH could have carried was of length zero, one, or greater than one; 11 is reserved.

fields.name: ArbitraryTag
fields.desc: Twelve bits of tag information, defaulting to 0 but configurable.

fields.name: AutonomousSystem
fields.desc: The AS number of the route, or 0 if the route is part of the local autonomous system.
